catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-moh:
An entry on Christian Mohr, a German sculptor born at Andernach in 1823 and dead at Cologne in 1888. He worked mainly at Cologne under cathedral architect Zwirner, settling there in 1845 after early ornamental work at Mainz and Koblenz. His first Cologne task was the tomb statuettes of Archbishop Conrad of Hochstaden, founder of the cathedral. Christ, the Evangelists, and fifty-nine angels figure on the south portal in his work.

On Emperor William the First's commission he carved eight statues for the middle hall, and his Saint Peter for the middle portal won a first-class medal at Paris in 1855. Beyond Cologne he made panoramic figures for Düsseldorf and thirty-four emperors for Aachen's town hall. Self-taught for the most part, he was also a collector of classical and German antiquities and wrote on Cologne's glory days and its gate towers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-mohr: This 1913 reference article on Mohr — the Silent Night priest. Joseph Otten honors his famous carol. His pen gave Christmas its song. The world sings the tender words. The nineteenth century knew his name. His 1848 death is famed. His 1818 carol is famed.

men-women-and-god-a-discussion-of-sex-qu:
The Reverend A. Herbert Gray wrote this guide to sex and marriage at the Student Christian Movement's request. He addresses students and young people directly, and speaks to men and women alike. His brother, Dr. Charles Gray, adds a medical appendix. Gray says plainly that he writes from a Christian point of view.

Gray argues that men and women must understand and help each other. He refuses to teach morality through fear, and leaves disease out of the book on purpose. Women friends advised him on the chapters aimed at women readers. The result is an unusually frank church guide from its era.
nasa-tm-19650019791-the-effect-of-materi:
Richard H Fish and James L Summers at Ames Research Center studied what happens when a fast particle strikes a thin plate. Their test asks a simple question with a hard answer. At what point does the impact just break through? That point is called the threshold condition for penetration, in their terms.

Thin plates of many metals were shot with small aluminum spheres. Speeds ranged from low up to eight and a half kilometers per second. The threshold idea helps judge impact resistance for spacecraft parts. Manned modules, pressure vessels, and fuel tanks all face the same risk from tiny high-speed debris in orbit.
nasa-tm-19680028472-electrical-stress-an:
Vincent R. Lalli of Lewis Research Center checks electric stress in a power unit for a microthruster in this November 1968 memo. Good power gear for propulsion tests was hard to get, he notes. Data from past space work showed some failures came from parts pushed past their safe stress.

Lalli tested the unit to find its worst over-stressed parts. The unit was then changed to remove those weak points. After the fix, it ran non-stop for more than seven thousand hours. The work shows how stress checks can turn a weak unit into a tough one. Small thrusters need power gear that lasts through long tests in space.
the-chums-of-scranton-high-out-for-the-p:
Donald Ferguson wrote this boys' baseball story about Scranton High in the Three Town League. Chapter I opens on a Thursday spoiled by rain. Practice is off, and only one more work-out stands between the boys and Saturday's game with Belleville.

The boys agree they need all the practice they can get. A visitor from Belleville reports that both his club and Allandale are stronger than last year. Each rival, rumor says, has set its heart on winning the championship. The contents promise a man trap, a painful shock for Scranton fans, Hugh's fade-away ball, and a glorious finish. Ferguson builds the tale on school loyalty, close games, and a mystery thread that runs beside the pennant race, in the manner of his other Scranton books.
